theory.title: TLS: The Encrypted Envelope
theory.recap: You can route, filter, and complete a TCP handshake. TLS is what the browser layers on top of TCP every time you see a padlock. The TCP handshake still happens first - then a second handshake negotiates encryption and verifies the server's identity through its certificate.
theory.plainObjective: Route to the HTTPS firewall, complete the TCP handshake, then complete the TLS handshake. The certificate step decides whether you trust the server.
theory.summary: This is what happens invisibly every time you visit an HTTPS site. The padlock in your browser means both the TCP and TLS handshakes completed and the server presented a valid certificate.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Why not just TCP?
bodyParagraphs.text: TCP delivers your packet reliably, but anyone on the path can read it. Every router, ISP, and network tap between you and the server sees plain text. TLS (Transport Layer Security) wraps the data in encryption so only the intended server - the one with the right private key - can read it.

bodyParagraphs.heading: TCP first, then TLS
bodyParagraphs.text: TLS doesn't replace TCP - it sits on top. You still complete the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) before TLS begins. Only over an ESTABLISHED TCP connection does the TLS handshake start. Two handshakes, one connection.

bodyParagraphs.heading: The TLS handshake
bodyParagraphs.text: Step 1: ClientHello - the client lists supported cipher suites and a random value. Step 2: ServerHello + Certificate - the server picks a cipher and proves its identity with a signed certificate. Step 3: ChangeCipherSpec - both sides derive matching session keys and confirm encryption is active.

bodyParagraphs.heading: Certificates and trust
bodyParagraphs.text: The certificate is the heart of TLS. A real CA signs the cert; your device trusts only certificates with valid signatures, matching domain names, and unexpired dates. Three certificate options sit ahead of you - one valid, one expired, one for the wrong domain. Pick the wrong one and the handshake aborts.

bodyParagraphs.heading: HTTPS = HTTP + TLS
bodyParagraphs.text: Port 80 sends HTTP as plain text. Port 443 wraps the same HTTP inside TLS. The application code does not change - only the transport layer differs. The port number signals to both sides that TLS must complete before any application data is exchanged.

theory.mission:
You carry port 443, destined for 10.40.1.10.

Route through R1, pass the HTTPS firewall, complete the TCP handshake, then begin TLS at ClientHello. Three certificates wait - two are invalid. Choose the valid one to reach ChangeCipherSpec and the secure server.

termIntroductions.headline: TLS
termIntroductions.body: TLS (Transport Layer Security) encrypts data in transit. Without it, every router between you and the server can read your traffic. With it, only the server holding the right private key can decrypt what you send. All HTTPS connections use TLS - and TLS always runs on top of TCP.

termIntroductions.headline: ClientHello
termIntroductions.body: ClientHello opens the TLS handshake - but only after TCP is ESTABLISHED. You tell the server which cipher suites you support and send a random value. The server will respond with its choice and its certificate. The handshake must follow this order.

termIntroductions.headline: Server Certificate
termIntroductions.body: The server sends its certificate - a signed document proving its identity. Your device checks the signature against trusted Certificate Authorities, the domain name on the cert, and the expiry date. Two of the three certs ahead fail one of those checks. Only one is valid.

termIntroductions.headline: Expired Certificate
termIntroductions.body: This certificate's validity period ended in 2019. Even though it's correctly signed and for the right domain, a TLS client rejects it as untrustworthy - the longer a cert is in circulation, the higher the chance its private key was leaked. This is why browsers warn you about expired certs.

termIntroductions.headline: Wrong-Domain Certificate
termIntroductions.body: This certificate is valid but for wrong.example - not the domain you're connecting to. An attacker presenting a real cert from a different domain cannot impersonate the real one. The hostname-match check is what stops most TLS spoofing attempts.

termIntroductions.headline: TLS Established
termIntroductions.body: ChangeCipherSpec signals that both sides have derived matching session keys from the handshake data. From this point, all traffic is encrypted. The server will now accept your application data - not as plain text, but as ciphertext only it can read.
